topics.title: Introduction and Factors Prompting Development of ABC
explain: Traditional costing pools overheads into cost centers and absorbs them using volume bases like labour hours or machine hours.
Using simple volume bases assumes longer production time generates higher overheads, which causes inaccurate costing.
Modern manufacturing uses high automation, leading to growing overhead costs relative to direct labour costs.
Four main factors prompted ABC: rising overheads, stiff market competition, product diversity, and cheaper IT data processing.

flow.title: Evolution from Traditional Costing to ABC
steps: Traditional costing groups overheads into cost centers
Overheads absorbed using labour or machine hours
Automation increases overheads and distorts unit costs
Demand grows for accurate activity-based allocation
ABC methodology developed for precise costing

topics.example: A fully automated plant incurs heavy machinery maintenance costs. Allocating these costs purely based on human labour hours distorts the true cost of making each item.
remember: Traditional absorption costing relies primarily on volume-based allocation (labour/machine hours).
Automation shifts cost structures from direct labour to high indirect overheads.
mistakes: Assuming traditional absorption costing is inaccurate for all businesses; it works fine when overheads are low or products are simple.

quiz.q: Which of the following factors prompted the development of Activity Based Costing?
o: Growing overhead costs due to automated production
quiz.why: Automated production leads to higher indirect overhead costs, requiring more precise allocation methods like ABC.

quiz.q: What is the primary cause of inaccuracy in traditional absorption costing?
o: Overhead rate based solely on volume drivers
quiz.why: Traditional costing assumes overheads are driven only by volume bases like labour or machine hours.

topics.title: Meaning, Definition, and Usefulness of ABC
explain: Activity Based Costing assigns costs to activities first, and then to products/services based on activity consumption.
CIMA defines ABC as an approach tracing resource consumption to activities and using cost drivers to assign costs to outputs.
ABC creates a clear link between resource consumption, activities, and final cost objects.
It is most suitable when overheads are high, product ranges are diverse, and stiff market competition exists.

flow.title: Two-Stage Cost Assignment in ABC
steps: Identify resources consumed by organization
Assign resource costs to specific activities
Determine activity cost drivers for pools
Assign activity costs to final cost objects

topics.example: Instead of spreading quality inspection costs across all products equally, ABC charges more inspection cost to a complex product that requires 10 inspections compared to a simple one needing only 1.
remember: ABC assigns costs to activities first, and then to cost objects.
ABC identifies non-value-adding activities to facilitate cost reduction.
mistakes: Thinking ABC is only useful for manufacturing; it is equally applicable to service and retail sectors.

quiz.q: According to CIMA definition, costs are assigned to cost objects in ABC based on:
quiz.why: CIMA defines ABC as assigning resource costs to activities and activity costs to outputs using cost drivers.

quiz.q: In which scenario is ABC MOST useful?
o: When overhead costs are extremely low
When a company makes a single uniform product
When non-volume related activities are present significantly
quiz.why: ABC excels when non-volume activities (like setups and inspections) drive substantial overhead costs across diverse products.

topics.title: Key Terms Used in ABC
explain: Activity: An event or task that consumes resources and incurs cost (e.g., machine setup, purchasing).
Cost Object: Any item for which cost measurement is required (e.g., product, customer, service, job).
Cost Pool: A group of individual cost items sharing the same cause-and-effect relationship.
Cost Driver: A factor that causes a change in the cost of an activity.
Resource Cost Driver measures resource consumption by activities; Activity Cost Driver measures demand on activities by cost objects.

flow.title: Hierarchy of ABC Elements
steps: Resources consumed by operations
Resource Cost Driver assigns to Activity Pool
Activity Cost Pool accumulates costs
Activity Cost Driver assigns to Cost Object

topics.example: For the activity 'Order Processing', the total cost of the purchasing department forms the Cost Pool, and the 'Number of Purchase Orders' acts as the Activity Cost Driver.
remember: Activity Driver: Links Activities -> Cost Objects.
mistakes: Confusing Resource Cost Drivers with Activity Cost Drivers.

quiz.q: A measure of the quantity of resources consumed by an activity is called a:
quiz.why: Resource cost drivers measure resource consumption by activities, whereas activity cost drivers measure consumption of activities by cost objects.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of an Activity Cost Driver for the 'Research and Development' business function?
quiz.why: The number of research projects directly causes variations in R&D activity costs.

topics.title: Cost Allocation: Traditional Costing vs ABC
explain: Traditional costing pools costs by functional departments (cost centers), whereas ABC pools costs by specific activities.
Traditional absorption relies on arbitrary volume bases (labour hours), while ABC uses activity-specific cost drivers.
Functional departments contain diverse activities behaving differently; ABC groups costs with identical cost behavior.
ABC eliminates cost distortion, ensuring low-volume complex products are not under-costed relative to high-volume products.

flow.title: Comparing Overhead Absorption Flow
steps: Overhead incurred in plant
Traditional: Allocate to Department Cost Centers
ABC: Group into Activity Cost Pools
Traditional: Absorb using Labour/Machine Hours
ABC: Absorb using Activity Cost Drivers

topics.example: Under traditional costing, a simple high-volume product absorbs most overheads because it takes more total labour hours, even if a low-volume custom product requires 90% of machine setup efforts.
remember: Traditional costing causes cross-subsidization (high volume over-costed, low volume under-costed).
ABC uses activities running across functional boundaries.
mistakes: Believing prime costs (direct material and direct labour) are treated differently in ABC; ABC primarily changes indirect overhead allocation.

quiz.q: In traditional absorption costing, overheads are first related to:
quiz.why: Traditional costing assigns overheads to departmental cost centers before absorbing them into products.

quiz.q: Under traditional volume-based costing, low-volume complex products are typically:
quiz.why: Low-volume products consume significant batch/product-level activities but absorb few overheads under volume bases, leading to under-costing.

topics.title: Level of Activities / Cost Hierarchy
explain: Cooper (1990) categorized activities into a 4-level cost hierarchy to identify appropriate cost drivers.
Unit Level: Performed each time a unit is produced (e.g., indirect materials, inspecting every unit).
Batch Level: Performed each time a batch is produced; costs are fixed per batch (e.g., machine setups, order processing).
Product Level: Performed to support specific product lines (e.g., product design, technical drawing updates).
Facility Level: Sustains general manufacturing processes and cannot be traced to specific products (e.g., building maintenance, plant security).

flow.title: The Four-Tier Cost Hierarchy
steps: Unit Level (Varies with units produced)
Batch Level (Varies with number of batches)
Product Level (Supports specific product line)
Facility Level (Sustains overall plant capability)

topics.example: Designing a new car model is a Product-level activity; setting up the assembly line for a run of 500 cars is a Batch-level activity; installing tires on one car is a Unit-level activity.
remember: Unit level costs scale directly with output volume.
Batch level costs are fixed for a batch but vary with the number of batches.
Facility level costs are common costs shared by all products.
mistakes: Treating batch setup costs as unit-level costs by dividing them directly over total output without considering batch sizes.

quiz.q: Designing product specifications and keeping technical drawings up to date are examples of:
quiz.why: Product-level activities support specific products regardless of units or batches produced.

quiz.q: Plant security and building maintenance belong to which activity level?
quiz.why: Facility-level activities sustain general factory operations and cannot be traced to specific units or products.

topics.title: Stages in ABC and Implementation Requirements
explain: Step 1 & 2: Identify activities within the firm and relate overheads to them to form cost pools.
Step 3: Re-apportion support activity costs to primary activities based on usage.
Step 4 & 5: Select activity cost drivers and calculate cost driver rates.
Cost Driver Rate Formula = Total Cost of Activity Pool / Total Activity Driver Units.
Implementation requirements: Staff training, process specification interviews, activity definition, cost driver selection, and cost assignment.

flow.title: Steps to Calculate Activity Driver Rate
steps: Identify and define organizational activities
Pool indirect costs into Activity Cost Pools
Identify primary activity cost drivers
Divide pool cost by total driver units
Apply rate to cost objects per consumption

topics.example: If the Machine Setup cost pool is ₹4,80,000 and total setups across all products are 50, the Cost Driver Rate is ₹4,80,000 / 50 = ₹9,600 per setup.
remember: Activity Cost Driver Rate = Total Activity Cost / Total Activity Driver Capacity.
mistakes: Forgetting to spread support activity costs across primary activities before computing the final driver rate.

quiz.q: What is the formula to calculate the Activity Cost Driver Rate?
o: Total Cost of Activity / Total Direct Labour Hours
Total Cost of Activity / Total Units of Activity Driver
Total Overhead Cost / Total Units Produced
Direct Material Cost / Number of Batches
quiz.why: The driver rate is calculated by dividing the total cost in an activity pool by the total activity driver units.

quiz.q: Which step is essential for securing workforce co-operation during ABC implementation?
quiz.why: Staff training creates awareness about the purpose of ABC and secures critical employee co-operation.

topics.title: Advantages and Limitations of ABC
explain: Advantages: Delivers accurate unit costs, logical overhead allocation, improved pricing, and non-value-adding activity identification.
Helps multi-product organizations understand true cost behavior across complex operations.
Limitations: Expensive and time-consuming to implement and maintain compared to traditional systems.
Selection of the most appropriate cost driver can be complex or subjective, and ABC is less beneficial for small single-product firms.

flow.title: Evaluating ABC Suitability
steps: Assess overhead proportion and product range
If high overheads & diverse products: Choose ABC
Identify non-value-adding cost reduction scope
Weigh implementation cost against benefits

topics.example: A company making 50 custom furniture models benefits immensely from ABC pricing accuracy, whereas a bakery making only one standard loaf of bread finds ABC unnecessarily expensive.
remember: ABC is ideal for multi-product firms with high overheads.
Key limitation: High cost of implementation and complexity in driver selection.
mistakes: Assuming ABC automatically reduces prime costs; ABC improves allocation and control of indirect overheads, not direct material/labour.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of Activity Based Costing?
quiz.why: ABC improves indirect overhead allocation and control; it does not directly alter prime costs (direct material and labour).

quiz.q: A major limitation of implementing ABC is that it:
o: Can only be used in service industries
Is more expensive and complex than traditional costing
quiz.why: ABC requires detailed data collection, making it costly and complex to set up and maintain.

topics.title: Practical Applications: ABM and ABB
explain: ABC as a Decision Tool: Aids product pricing, vendor evaluation, expansion planning, and branch performance evaluation.
Activity Based Management (ABM): Uses ABC information to manage activities and continuously improve customer value.
ABM Analyses: Cost Driver Analysis, Activity Analysis (Value-Added vs Non-Value-Added), and Performance Analysis.
Value-Added (VA) activities are indispensable tasks customers pay for (e.g., polishing furniture); Non-Value-Added (NVA) activities add cost without value (e.g., storing, moving materials).
Activity Based Budgeting (ABB): Reverses the ABC process to forecast resource needs based on budgeted activity workloads.

flow.title: Flow of Activity Based Management (ABM)
steps: Gather activity cost data via ABC
Classify activities as VA or NVA
Analyze root causes via cost drivers
Streamline operations & eliminate NVA tasks
Enhance process efficiency and customer value

topics.example: Moving raw materials across three storehouses before processing is a Non-Value-Added (NVA) activity. ABM targets this movement for elimination to save costs.
remember: ABM = Cost management application of ABC.
ABB = Reversing the ABC process for planning and budgeting.
Three key elements of ABB: Type, Quantity, and Cost of work to be done.
mistakes: Confusing VA and NVA activities; test whether the customer is willing to pay for the activity.

quiz.q: The management discipline that uses ABC cost data to improve efficiency and eliminate non-value-added activities is called:
quiz.why: ABM is the application of ABC cost information to manage activities and optimize business processes.

quiz.q: Which of the following is considered a Non-Value-Added (NVA) activity in a manufacturing plant?
quiz.why: Material movement adds handling cost without increasing the product's value or utility to the customer.
